nameStory: Alpine thyme-moss gets its name from two key features: it thrives in high-elevation alpine environments, and its tiny leaves are arranged in a way that resembles the herb thyme. The 'moss' part is obvious, but that alpine connection tells you exactly where to look for this rare treasure - way up in New England's mountains where the air is thin and the growing season is short.
description: Alpine thyme-moss is a small, cushion-forming moss that creates neat, compact patches in mountain habitats. It grows as dense mats of tiny stems covered in overlapping leaves that look almost scale-like when dry. This moss is quite rare in New England, with only a couple of documented locations, making it a special find for mountain explorers. Like most mosses, it stays green year-round but becomes more vibrant when wet.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms tight, cushion-like mats that feel springy underfoot when moist, becoming crisp and brittle when dry

idTips.label: Leaves

idTips.label: Color

idTips.label: Texture

habitat: Alpine thyme-moss lives in the harshest mountain environments New England has to offer - think above treeline on peaks like Mount Washington or other high summits. It grows on rocky alpine soils, often in areas that experience extreme temperature swings, strong winds, and short growing seasons. You'll find it nestled between rocks or in small soil pockets where snow lingers late into spring.

seasonality.spring: Becomes vibrant green as mountain snows melt, often one of the first signs of life in the alpine zone. This is when it's most noticeable and easiest to spot against the brown, winter-worn landscape.
seasonality.summer: Remains green and active during the brief alpine growing season, taking advantage of every moment of warmth and moisture. Sporophytes may develop during this peak growing time.
seasonality.fall: Begins to slow growth as temperatures drop, but stays green. May become less vibrant as it prepares for the long mountain winter.
seasonality.winter: Survives under snow cover, remaining alive but dormant. Often completely buried and invisible until spring melt reveals the still-green cushions.

funFact: This moss is actually a natural hybrid - like a plant mule - created when two other moss species mixed their genetics through a rare process that scientists once thought was impossible in mosses, making it a living example of evolutionary innovation happening right under our feet!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other cushion-forming alpine mosses, but the high-elevation habitat narrows it down significantly. Remember: if you're not above treeline or very close to it, you're probably looking at a different moss species entirely.
contextualKnowledge: With only 2 recorded observations in all of New England, this is one of our rarest mosses. Finding it would be a significant botanical discovery worth reporting to local naturalist groups or botanical surveys.
compareHints: Unlike its relatives Woodsy Thyme-moss (found in forests) and Marsh Thyme-moss (found in wetlands), Alpine thyme-moss is strictly a high-elevation specialist. Wavy-leaf Moss has more obvious leaf margins and typically grows in different habitats. The alpine habitat is really your best clue - if you're not gasping for breath from the altitude, you're probably looking at one of its lowland cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its thyme-moss relatives, Woodsy Thyme-moss has the most orderly, shingle-like leaf arrangement compared to Wavy-leaf Moss's more irregular, wavy-edged leaves.

Wavy-leaf Moss stands out from its thyme-moss relatives primarily by those distinctive wavy, toothed leaf margins - Woodsy Thyme-moss has smoother leaf edges, while Marsh Thyme-moss prefers wetter areas and has more pointed leaves.
Compared to its relatives, Marsh Thyme-moss has the broadest, most elliptical leaves - Woodsy Thyme-moss has more pointed leaves, while Wavy-leaf Moss has distinctly wavy leaf edges.
